sword_marker_records.content_osis: <div sID="gen8699" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="10" osisID="Ezra.10" sID="Ezra.10"/> <div eID="gen8699" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8700" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen8701" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we have that grievance redressed which was complained of and lamented in the foregoing chapter. Observe, I. How the people's hearts were prepared for the redress of it by their deep humiliation for the sin, <reference osisRef="Ezra.10.1">ver. 1</reference>. II. How it was proposed to Ezra by Shechaniah, <reference osisRef="Ezra.10.2-Ezra.10.4">ver. 2-4</reference>. III. How the proposal was put in execution. 1. The great men were sworn to stand to it, <reference osisRef="Ezra.10.5">ver. 5</reference>. 2. Ezra appeared first in it, <reference osisRef="Ezra.10.6">ver. 6</reference>. 3. A general assembly was called, <reference osisRef="Ezra.10.7-Ezra.10.9">ver. 7-9</reference>. 4. They all, in compliance with Ezra's exhortation, agreed to the reformation, <reference osisRef="Ezra.10.10-Ezra.10.14">ver. 10-14</reference>. 5. Commissioners were appointed to sit "de die in diem"—day after day, to enquire who had married strange wives and to oblige them to put them away, which was done accordingly (<reference osisRef="Ezra.10.15-Ezra.10.17">ver. 15-17</reference>), and a list of the names of those that were found guilty given in, <reference osisRef="Ezra.10.18-Ezra.10.44">ver. 18-44</reference>.

(<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 456.)</title> <div sID="gen8702" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Now when Ezra had prayed, and when he had confessed, weeping and casting himself down before the house of God, there assembled unto him out of Israel a very great congregation of men and women and children: for the people wept very sore. <hi type="super">2</hi> And Shechaniah the son of Jehiel, <hi type="italic">one</hi> of the sons of Elam, answered and said unto Ezra, We have trespassed against our God, and have taken strange wives of the people of the land: yet now there is hope in Israel concerning this thing. <hi type="super">3</hi> Now therefore let us make a covenant with our God to put away all the wives, and such as are born of them, according to the counsel of my lord, and of those that tremble at the commandment of our God; and let it be done according to the law. <hi type="super">4</hi> Arise; for <hi type="italic">this</hi> matter <hi type="italic">belongeth</hi> unto thee: we also <hi type="italic">will be</hi> with thee: be of good courage, and do <hi type="italic">it.</hi> <hi type="super">5</hi> Then arose Ezra, and made the chief priests, the Levites, and all Israel, to swear that they should do according to this word. And they sware. <div eID="gen8702" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8703" type="x-p"/> We are here told, <div eID="gen8703" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8704" type="x-p"/> I. What good impressions were made upon the people by Ezra's humiliation and confession of sin. No sooner was it noised in the city that their new governor, in whom they rejoiced, was himself in grief, and to so great a degree, for them and their sin, than presently there <hi type="italic">assembled to him a very great congregation,</hi> to see what the matter was and to mingle their tears with his, <reference osisRef="Ezra.10.1">v. 1</reference>. Our weeping for other people's sins may perhaps set those a weeping for them themselves who otherwise would continue senseless and remorseless. See what a happy influence the good examples of great ones may have upon their inferiors. When Ezra, a scribe, a scholar, a man in authority under the king, so deeply lamented the public corruptions, they concluded that they were indeed very grievous, else he would not thus have grieved for them; and this drew tears from every eye: <hi type="italic">men, women, and children, wept very sore,</hi> when he wept thus. <div eID="gen8704" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8705" type="x-p"/> II. What a good motion Shechaniah made upon this occasion. The place was <hi type="italic">Bochim</hi>—a place of <hi type="italic">weepers;</hi> but, for aught that appears, there was a profound silence among them, as among Job's friends, who <hi type="italic">spoke not a word to him, because they saw that his grief was very great,</hi> till Shechaniah (one of Ezra's companions from Babylon, <reference osisRef="Ezra.8.3">ch. viii. 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezra.8.5">5</reference>) stood up, and made a speech addressed to Ezra, in which, <div eID="gen8705" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8706" type="x-p"/> 1. He owns the national guilt, sums up all Ezra's confession in one word, and sets to his seal that it is true: "<hi type="italic">We have trespassed against our God, and have taken strange wives,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezra.10.2">v. 2</reference>. The matter is too plain to be denied and too bad to be excused." It does not appear that Shechaniah was himself culpable in this matter (if he had had the beam in his own eye, he could not have seen so clearly to pluck it out of his brother's eye), but his father was guilty, and several of his father's house (as appears <reference osisRef="Ezra.10.26">v. 26</reference>), and therefore he reckons himself among the trespassers; nor does he seek to excuse or palliate the sin, though some of his own relations were guilty of it, but, in the cause of God, <hi type="italic">says to his father, I have not known him,</hi> as Levi, <reference osisRef="Deut.33.9">Deut. xxxiii. 9</reference>. Perhaps the strange wife that his father had married had been an unjust unkind step-mother to him, and had made mischief in the family, and he supposed that others had done the like, which made him the more forward to appear against this corruption; if so, this was not the only time that private resentments have been over ruled by the providence of God to serve the public good. <div eID="gen8706" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8707" type="x-p"/> 2. He encourages himself and others to hope that though the matter was bad it might be amended: <hi type="italic">Yet now there is hope in Israel</hi> (where else should there be hope but in Israel? those that are strangers to that commonwealth are said to have <hi type="italic">no hope,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.2.12">Eph. ii. 12</reference>) even <hi type="italic">concerning this thing.</hi> The case is sad, but it is not desperate; the disease is threatening, but not incurable. There is hope that the people may be reformed, the guilty reclaimed, a stop put to the spreading of the contagion; and so the judgments which the sin deserves may be prevented and all will be well. <hi type="italic">Now there is hope;</hi> now that the disease is discovered it is half-cured. Now that the alarm is taken the people begin to be sensible of the mischief, and to lament it, a spirit of repentance seems to be poured out upon them, and they are all thus humbling themselves before God for it, <hi type="italic">now there is hope</hi> that God will forgive, and have mercy. The <hi type="italic">valley of Achor</hi> (that is, of <hi type="italic">trouble</hi>) is the <hi type="italic">door of hope</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hos.2.15">Hos. ii. 15</reference>); for the sin that truly troubles us shall not ruin us. There is hope now that Israel has such a prudent, pious, zealous governor as Ezra to manage this affair. Note, (1.) In melancholy times we must see and observe what makes for us, as well as what makes against us. (2.) There may be good hopes through grace, even when there is the sense of great guilt before God. (3.) Where sin is seen and lamented, and good steps are taken towards a reformation, even sinners ought to be encouraged. (4.) Even great saints must thankfully receive seasonable counsel and comfort from those that are much their inferiors, as Ezra from Shechaniah. <div eID="gen8707" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8708" type="x-p"/> 3. He advises that a speedy and effectual course should be taken for the divorcing of the strange wives. Declare it to be the sense of all the sober serious people among us, which cannot but have a great sway among Israelites." (2.) (3.) "While we are in a good mind, let us bind ourselves by a solemn vow and covenant that we will do it, lest, when the present impressions are worn off, the thing be left undone. Let us covenant, not only that, if we have strange wives ourselves, we will put them away, but that, if we have not, we will do what we can in our places to oblige others to put away theirs." (4.) And they sware. <div eID="gen8702" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8703" type="x-p"/> We are here told, <div eID="gen8703" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8704" type="x-p"/> I. What good impressions were made upon the people by Ezra's humiliation and confession of sin. No sooner was it noised in the city that their new governor, in whom they rejoiced, was himself in grief, and to so great a degree, for them and their sin, than presently there <hi type="italic">assembled to him a very great congregation,</hi> to see what the matter was and to mingle their tears with his, <reference osisRef="Ezra.10.1">v. 1</reference>. Our weeping for other people's sins may perhaps set those a weeping for them themselves who otherwise would continue senseless and remorseless. See what a happy influence the good examples of great ones may have upon their inferiors. When Ezra, a scribe, a scholar, a man in authority under the king, so deeply lamented the public corruptions, they concluded that they were indeed very grievous, else he would not thus have grieved for them; and this drew tears from every eye: <hi type="italic">men, women, and children, wept very sore,</hi> when he wept thus. <div eID="gen8704" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8705" type="x-p"/> II. What a good motion Shechaniah made upon this occasion. The place was <hi type="italic">Bochim</hi>—a place of <hi type="italic">weepers;</hi> but, for aught that appears, there was a profound silence among them, as among Job's friends, who <hi type="italic">spoke not a word to him, because they saw that his grief was very great,</hi> till Shechaniah (one of Ezra's companions from Babylon, <reference osisRef="Ezra.8.3">ch. viii. 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezra.8.5">5</reference>) stood up, and made a speech addressed to Ezra, in which, <div eID="gen8705" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8706" type="x-p"/> 1. He owns the national guilt, sums up all Ezra's confession in one word, and sets to his seal that it is true: "<hi type="italic">We have trespassed against our God, and have taken strange wives,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezra.10.2">v. 2</reference>. Perhaps the strange wife that his father had married had been an unjust unkind step-mother to him, and had made mischief in the family, and he supposed that others had done the like, which made him the more forward to appear against this corruption; if so, this was not the only time that private resentments have been over ruled by the providence of God to serve the public good. <div eID="gen8706" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8707" type="x-p"/> 2. He encourages himself and others to hope that though the matter was bad it might be amended: <hi type="italic">Yet now there is hope in Israel</hi> (where else should there be hope but in Israel? those that are strangers to that commonwealth are said to have <hi type="italic">no hope,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.2.12">Eph. ii. 12</reference>) even <hi type="italic">concerning this thing.</hi> The case is sad, but it is not desperate; the disease is threatening, but not incurable. He puts them in a good method for the effecting of this reformation, and shows them not only that it must be done, but how. (1.) "Let Ezra, and all those that are present in this assembly, agree in a resolution that this must be done (pass a vote immediately to this effect: it will now pass <hi type="italic">nemine contradicente—unanimously</hi>), that it may be said to be done <hi type="italic">according to the counsel of my lord,</hi> the president of the assembly, with the unanimous concurrence of those that <hi type="italic">tremble at the commandment of our God,</hi> which is the description of those that were gathered to him, <reference osisRef="Ezra.9.4">ch. ix. 4</reference>. "Let the command of God in this matter, which Ezra recited in his prayer, be laid before the people, and let them see that it is <hi type="italic">done according to the law;</hi> we have that to warrant us, nay, that binds us to what we do; it is not an addition of our own to the divine law, but the necessary execution of it."
